hook: I have walked this house with clients, alone, and trailing a whole pack of other agents, and it gets me every single time.
story: I have walked this property more times than I can count, with clients, completely alone just to sit with it, and more than once trailing a pack of other agents on caravan, and every single time it does something to me. 2666 Aberdeen sits on nearly an acre and a half in the Los Feliz hills, a 1922 Spanish Colonial Revival designed by Stiles O. Clements that made its Architectural Digest debut two years after it was finished. Hand-painted beams, stained glass windows, terraced grounds with a pool, spa, and koi pond, and yes, an actual passageway to a speakeasy behind a vault door. One of my favorite versions of this house was staged by Franchesca Grace. I did not think it could get more beautiful or more mystical than it already was, and then I walked in and it had. If you want to see it for yourself, I'd love to show you.
listingAgentCredit: Listed by Ben Belack, Serhant California, Inc

hook: If you want to be a Disney princess in real life, this is the house you buy.
story: This one made the list the second I stepped past the ivy and found a water wheel still turning against the side of the house. 485 Madeline Drive was built in 1910 as the tea house for Busch Gardens, the 32-acre botanical wonderland that once sat on some of Pasadena's most coveted land before it closed in 1937, and this storybook English cottage is the last trace of it still standing. Leaded stained glass, hand-carved millwork, a two-story lofted basement, gardens that wind past stone steps and a little bridge under the trees. It is the kind of house that makes you stop mid-sentence the moment you walk in, and that is exactly the feeling I want for whoever ends up living there. If it's speaking to you the way it spoke to me, I'd love to talk it through.
listingAgentCredit: Listed by Bryony Atkinson & Abigail Dotson, MAISONRE

hook: The kitchen is anchored by a slab of Viola Calacatta Monet marble so dramatic the custom cabinetry around it just reads as backup.
story: This one made the list for the kitchen, or really for the slab of Viola Calacatta Monet marble anchoring it, veined and dramatic enough that everything else in the room feels like it was chosen to frame it rather than compete with it. The primary suite picks the same thread back up, more of that Viola marble alongside handcrafted Zia tile that adds real texture, the kind that never quite comes through in photos. It's a fully new build, but somebody clearly cared about restraint on the outside as much as drama on the inside, custom wood siding, quiet architectural lines, and two genuinely old olive trees left standing right at the entry instead of cleared out for a cleaner build. Out back it's a proper retreat, a stone-wrapped pool and spa, a custom cabana, and an outdoor kitchen built for actual use, not just photos. It sits on a quiet, tree-lined street walkable to Kester Magnet School, minutes from Ventura Boulevard, the kind of block that still feels like an actual neighborhood this close to everything. If a marble kitchen like that is the kind of detail that gets you, tell me and let's go see it.

hook: Every room here seems to be arguing over which view is better, the canyon from the living room or the sunset from the primary suite's own balcony.
story: This one made the list for the view, which is not a small claim for a 1956 post-and-beam that already has real architectural pedigree behind it. Richard Dorman designed it for the Modern Trend Construction Company, and the walls of glass in the living room open the whole space to canyon and hillside that just keeps unfolding, while the primary suite steps straight out to its own private balcony over that same view, no detour required. It sits on nearly an acre north of Mulholland, on the cusp of Bel Air and Sherman Oaks, gated and quiet, and it's been restored down to the studs, new roof, new electrical, all new plumbing, owned Tesla solar, while the bones stay exactly as intentional as they were in 1956. The kitchen is where I'd actually want to cook, anchored by a baby blue LaCanche range I would build a dinner party around, terrazzo tile pulled straight from the original terrazzo they uncovered during the restoration. Outside it keeps going too, pool, fire pit, a covered outdoor kitchen, fruit trees, and a powder room wallpapered in Gucci I still think about. If a view like that and a range that color sound like your kind of house, let's talk.

hook: The firewood is stacked into its own wall by the front door, which tells you everything about how seriously this house takes being lived in.
story: This one made the list because of the firewood, stacked floor to ceiling in its own little alcove right by the front door, like whoever built this place assumed you'd actually be here through a real winter and wanted you covered before you even got your coat off. Paul R. Williams designed it in 1924, the same architect behind half of the houses in this city people still stop their cars for, and it's known as The Flint House, one of the real Pasadena landmarks instead of just another big Spanish number in the hills. Hand-troweled stucco, a terracotta barrel tile roof, Saltillo tile underfoot, wrought iron everywhere it should be and nowhere it shouldn't. There's a study with built-in shelving that runs floor to ceiling and its own rolling ladder, which is the kind of detail you can't fake with a renovation, and three ensuite bedrooms that each step out onto their own private balcony over the canyon. It sits on seven-tenths of an acre with a pool, an outdoor kitchen, and a view that stretches well past the Rose Bowl on a clear day. If Paul Williams and a wall of firewood sound like your kind of house, let's talk.

hook: The courtyard cactus is taller than the roofline, and that's not even the best reason this one's on the list.
story: This one made the list because of the cactus, which sounds like an odd reason to fall for a house until you actually see it, guarding the courtyard gate, grown taller than the roofline because somebody decided decades ago it got to keep going instead of getting cut back to a tidy size, and that tells you everything about how this place has actually been cared for. It went up in 1922, built of adobe and designed by architect Harwood Hewitt, and it is both Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 621 and part of the West Adams Terrace HPOZ—which is a fancy way of saying nobody gets to erase what makes it what it is. Walk in and the original tile is still doing its job at the base of the stairs, the ceilings are wood-beamed, the hardwood floors have a hundred years of actual life in them, and the kitchen's been brought current without stripping any of that out. If a house with real history instead of six months of staging is what you're after, tell me and let's go see it.
listingAgentCredit: Listed by Molly Kelley & Daria Greenbaum, Compass
